title: Inheritance and polymorphism
subtitle: Reuse a class, specialise it, and let one call do the right thing for every kind of object.

sections.title: Inheritance
sections.body: class Dog : public Animal makes Dog a specialisation of Animal: it inherits Animal’s members and may add or replace some. Use it for “is-a” relationships (a Dog is an Animal); use composition (a member object) for “has-a” (a Car has an Engine). Public inheritance is the usual form; private members of the base stay inaccessible to the derived class, protected ones are visible.

questions.prompt: Which fits composition (has-a) rather than inheritance?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A car has an engine; it is not one.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — inheritance
figures.note: Arrows point from the specialised class to the general one.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
{Animal | name | speak()} as a
{Dog | breed | fetch()} as d
{Cat | indoor | purr()} as c
d -> a : is-a
c -> a : is-a");

sections.title: Constructor and destructor order
sections.body: Creating a derived object runs the base constructor first, then the derived one; destruction is the reverse (derived destructor first, then base). The base part must exist before the derived part can rely on it.

questions.prompt: Destroying a Derived object calls destructors in the order…

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — construction order
figures.note: Build from the foundation up, tear down in reverse.

sections.title: Overriding and hiding
sections.body: A derived class can redefine a base method. Without virtual the version chosen depends on the declared (static) type of the pointer or reference; with virtual it depends on the actual object type. Multiple inheritance (several bases) is allowed but can cause the diamond problem; virtual base classes solve it.

questions.prompt: Without virtual, Animal* p = new Dog(); p->speak(); calls…

sections.title: Virtual functions and dynamic dispatch
sections.body: Declare the base method virtual and the call through a base pointer runs the override of the actual object. Internally each object with virtual functions carries a hidden pointer (vptr) to its class’s table (vtable) of function addresses; the call looks up the slot at run time.

worked.why: Three objects in an Animal* array: Dog, Cat, Cow, each overriding speak().
One loop calling p[i]->speak() produces three different outputs — no if/else on type.

questions.prompt: Dynamic dispatch chooses the function by…

choices.text: The actual type of the object at run time.

figures.caption: Figure 6.1.1 — virtual dispatch
figures.note: The vtable sends the call to Dog::speak; Animal::speak is never used.

sections.title: Abstract classes and virtual destructors
sections.body: A pure virtual function (virtual double area() = 0;) has no body and makes the class abstract — it cannot be instantiated and acts as an interface that derived classes must implement. Always give a polymorphic base a virtual destructor, or delete through a base pointer skips the derived destructor and leaks.

worked.why: Areas via one loop over Shape*: 3.14·2² = 12.56 and 15; total 27.56.

questions.prompt: A class with a pure virtual function…

figures.caption: Figure 6.2.1 — abstract Shape
figures.note: Each concrete shape supplies its own area().
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
{Shape (abstract) | | area() = 0 ; virtual ~Shape()} as s
{Circle | r | area()} as c
{Rect | w ; h | area()} as r
c -> s
r -> s");

problems.prompt: Why must the base class destructor be virtual when objects are deleted through base pointers?
problems.answer: Otherwise only the base destructor runs, so the derived part is never cleaned up (leak/undefined behaviour).

sections.title: Late binding cost and design tips
sections.body: A virtual call costs one extra indirection and prevents inlining; it is negligible except in tight loops. Prefer small interfaces, favour composition over deep hierarchies, and mark overrides with override so the compiler catches signature mismatches.

choices.text: Making the compiler check you really override a virtual function.
